nameStory: The 'lyreleaf' name comes from the shape of this plant's distinctive leaves, which resemble a lyre - that ancient harp-like musical instrument. The leaves are widest at the tip with smaller lobes extending down the sides, just like the curved arms of a lyre. It's also called 'wild sage' because it belongs to the same genus as culinary sage, though it's our native North American version.
description: Lyreleaf sage is a low-growing perennial wildflower that forms rosettes of unusual leaves close to the ground. In spring, it sends up slender flower spikes about 1-2 feet tall topped with small purple or blue flowers. The plant is most recognizable by its distinctively shaped leaves that stay green through much of the year. As a member of the mint family, it has the characteristic square stems and two-lipped flowers that make mints easy to spot.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive lyre-shaped leaves form a ground-hugging rosette. The leaves are broadest at the tip with smaller rounded lobes extending down the sides, creating that musical instrument silhouette. Feel the leaves - they're somewhat fuzzy and have a slightly rough texture.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small purple, blue, or sometimes white flowers arranged in loose spikes on square stems. Each flower has the typical mint family shape with two lips - an upper hood and a lower landing platform for bees. The flowers have a light, pleasant fragrance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low rosettes of leaves pressed close to the ground, with flower stalks rising 1-2 feet above. The plant spreads slowly by underground runners, sometimes forming small colonies in ideal spots.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Flower stems are distinctly four-sided (square in cross-section), a telltale sign of the mint family. Run your fingers along the stem to feel the sharp edges - they're quite pronounced and easy to detect.

idTips.label: Leaves (texture)
idTips.description: Leaves feel soft and slightly velvety due to fine hairs, with prominent veins creating a somewhat wrinkled appearance. They often have a grayish-green color and may show purple tinges, especially in cooler weather.

habitat: Lyreleaf sage thrives in open woodlands, woodland edges, and clearings with partial shade to full sun. It prefers well-drained, sandy or rocky soils and is often found in areas that are too dry for many other wildflowers. Look for it in oak-pine forests, along woodland trails, and in sunny spots within otherwise shaded areas.

seasonality.spring: Flower spikes emerge in late spring, typically May through early June, rising above the evergreen rosettes. This is the best time to spot the plant when the purple-blue flowers make it most visible.
seasonality.summer: After flowering, the plant focuses on leaf growth and may produce new rosettes. The distinctive lyre-shaped leaves remain the best identification feature during the hot months.
seasonality.fall: Leaves often develop purple or reddish tinges as temperatures cool. The rosettes remain visible and identifiable, though less conspicuous without flowers.
seasonality.winter: In milder winters, the tough rosettes persist and remain green under snow. Even when partially dormant, the distinctive leaf shape makes identification possible during winter thaws.

funFact: Despite being called 'wild sage' and belonging to the same genus as kitchen sage, lyreleaf sage was historically known as 'cancerweed' because Native Americans and early settlers used it medicinally - though modern science doesn't support these traditional cancer treatments, so please admire but don't self-medicate!
confusionNotes: The distinctive lyre-shaped leaves make this plant hard to confuse with anything else once you know what to look for. Beginners might mistake the low rosettes for young plantain or other basal-leaved plants, but the fuzzy texture and unique leaf shape with those side lobes are giveaways - remember the musical instrument!
contextualKnowledge: This is an extremely rare find in New England - it's at the very northern edge of its range here, with only one recorded observation in the region. If you think you've found lyreleaf sage in New England, take photos and consider reporting it to local botanists, as it would be a significant discovery. The plant is much more common in the southeastern United States.
compareHints: Lyreleaf sage is the only Salvia species you're likely to encounter in New England, making it unique in the region. Unlike its relatives such as garden sage, it forms ground-hugging rosettes rather than shrubby growth, and its flowers are much smaller and more delicate. The lyre-shaped leaves are completely distinctive within the sage genus - no other Salvia has this violin-like leaf form.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike lyreleaf sage which has distinctive lobed basal leaves and prefers shady woods, giant blue sage has narrow, unlobed leaves and demands full sun.
Unlike other sages that might be found in New England gardens like lyreleaf sage (which has much broader, lobed leaves), mintweed has very narrow, simple leaves and a weedy appearance.
Unlike native New England sages like lyreleaf sage, chia is much taller and more robust, growing 3-5 feet compared to the 1-2 foot height of most regional relatives.
Unlike our native Lyreleaf Sage which has deeply lobed leaves and purple flowers, Sticky Sage has simple heart-shaped leaves and yellow flowers.
Unlike the native lyreleaf sage with its small purple flowers and basal rosette of leaves, anise-scented sage forms tall bushy plants with much larger, intensely blue flowers.
